Abstract
Supercapacitors (SCs) are promising energy-storage systems whose efficiency largely depends on electrode composition 
and design. Utilizing carbon waste is vital for advancing sustainable technologies due to its high storage capacity, low cost, 
wide availability and eco-friendly nature. Biomass-derived carbon materials, with their high surface area, conductivity 
and environmental benefits, have emerged as strong candidates for next-generation SC electrodes. This review presents a 
systematic analysis of recent strategies for converting biomass waste into high-performance electrode materials for SCs. 
In addition, this summarizes an innovative thematic area where activated carbon is derived from novel sources like peanut 
shells, jujube shells, tea and coffee waste, hazelnuts, leather waste, paper waste etc. In addition, it encompasses the prepa -
ration of carbon-based products and strategies for enhancing porous structures by activation. Incorporating these materi -
als in SCs offers the dual benefit of enhancing energy storage performance while contributing to waste management and 
resource recycling. Importantly, this review introduces the novel concept of electrochemical double-layer compression due 
to solvated radicals, which modifies classical Helmholtz theory which has no prior literature. We further discuss the role of 
sequential chemical and physical activation in tuning porosity and ion transport with unique design proposal of sequential 
activation. Furthermore, future research directions are highlighted, zeroing in on promoting the scalability, electrochemi -
cal double-layer capacitor performance, and commercial credibility of such electrodes with the effects of impurities and 
quality control. This approach contributes to the development of low-cost, sustainable and scalable energy storage systems.
Keywords Supercapacitors · Energy storage devices · Biomass activated carbon · Carbon waste · EDLC

SCs are a popular choice over conventional capacitors 
owing to their ability to store a greater quantity of energy. 
The interface between the electrolyte and electrode plays a 
crucial role in facilitating charge separation within the elec-
tric double layer. The existence of a significant number of 
pores resulted in an enhanced surface area, enabling stor -
age to a comparatively higher extent of charge. This rapid

The SCs performance is heavily reliant on the electrode 
material (Fig. 3). Extensive research has been conducted 
to search for potential materials for electrodes, resulting 
in significant progress in both the fundamental and applied 
aspects of SCs. This study focuses on the potential use of 
carbon and its unwanted waste, owing to its abundance, 
affordability, ease of manufacture, eco-friendliness, good 
specific surface area, good mechanical properties, excellent 
ionic conductivity, better chemical stability, and wide range 
of operating temperature. High-end SC applications include 
electric and hybrid vehicles for rapid power delivery and 
regenerative braking, systems in aerospace and defense 
that are in need of reliable high-power bursts, and load bal-
ancing and backup power in grid-scale renewable energy 
systems. Other new applications include wearable electron-
ics, IoT devices, and high-frequency power stabilization in 
advanced electronic circuits [1–7].
  
Exigency of waste management as a 
material for SC electrodes
In recent years, there has been significant scholarly interest 
in the properties of carbon and its derivatives, particularly 
in relation to their exceptional capacity for electrochemical 
energy storage. Carbon allotropes exhibit a range of dimen-
sionalities (0D to 3D), influencing electrochemical behavior 
[8–11].
Carbon-based electrodes demonstrate excellent polariz -
ability, and the amphoteric nature of carbon further facili -
tates its electrochemical properties, allowing transitions 
between the donor and acceptor states. Moreover, it is sig -
nificant that carbon is primarily environmentally benign 
and chemically stable [ 8, 9]. Carbon electrodes are widely 
used because of their easy accessibility and processability. 
Carbon-based electrodes are stable in both acidic as well as 
basic solutions & they are able to be operated effectively 
across a vast temperatures range. Through several physical 
activation techniques, it is feasible to synthesize a substance 
with a significantly controlled surface morphology. This 
plays a critical role in determining the electrode/electrolyte 
interface for electrochemical energy applications, making 
carbon electrodes highly advantageous for electrochemical 
capacitor energy storage. Understanding surface functional

AC, a carbon-based non-hazardous material, possesses 
a porous structure and an exceptionally specific surface. 
Chemically, its structure resembles a crude graphite form, 
exhibiting an amorphous structure with a porous nature in 
the molecular range to visible cavities. The treatment of AC 
primarily relies on adsorption, in which the liquid or gas 
molecules adsorb on the internal and external surface walls 
of the material [14]. The substantial internal surface area of 
AC makes it suitable for adsorption. Furthermore, activated 
carbon is infused with specific compounds to optimize its 
properties for various applications, including the applied 
potential. As the current discussion pertains to electrode 
materials based on carbon, electrochemical double-layer 
behavior is expected for SC.
In addition, microcapacitors (MCs) serve as a corner -
stone in the domain of energy storage and power manage -
ment systems, particularly in applications that require high 
power density and rapid charge/discharge sequences. Tra -
ditionally, these devices employ carbon materials, such as 
AC, graphite, or CNTs, as electrodes. However, the incorpo-
ration of biomass and waste-derived carbonaceous materi -
als to produce MCs is a viable and sustainable alternative. 
This approach not only provides a green and economical 
solution but also reduces the dependence on non-renewable 
resources. Consequently, there is a need to explore biomass 
and its by-products as potential carbon materials for the fab-
rication of MCs. In addition to the aforementioned consid -
erations, there are several challenges associated with scaling 
these materials for potential applications in SCs, MCs, and 
other related devices [6, 15–17].
 ● Cost of Processing: Optimization of the conversion pro-
cess for biomass and waste into viable carbon materials 
is crucial for mitigating energy consumption and mini -
mizing costs, particularly in the context of large-scale 
production.
 ● Material Handling: The handling and processing of bio-
mass-derived carbons can present challenges owing to 
their heterogeneous characteristics. To address this is -
sue, it is essential to develop advanced processing tech-
niques that ensure the uniformity of these carbon mate -
rials and make them suitable for electrode fabrication.
 ● Consistency and Quality Control: Ensuring that bio -
mass-derived carbon materials retain their high-quality 
characteristics, such as surface area and porosity, during 
the scale-up process is essential. Variations in the feed -
stock, processing conditions, and post-treatment steps 
can significantly influence the performance of the final 
product.

cal for predicting double-layer behavior. The superficial 
functionalities of porous activated carbon (AC) nanospheres 
are vital in influencing the capacitive behavior, as they affect 
the wettability of the carbon surface through the electrolyte, 
resulting in pseudo-capacitance. Additionally, nanoporous 
carbons produced using template methods offer well-opti -

Biomass, a form of renewable natural energy derived 
from flora and fauna, consists of carbohydrates with rela -
tively fewer energy storage issues compared to other natural 
sources such as sun, tides, and wind. Authentic sources of 
biomass include agricultural waste, agro-industrial waste, 
municipal waste, and certain crops such as sugarcane, corn, 
and wheat. Woody biomass is collectively hemicellulose 
lignin and cellulose, in varying fractions cited as lignocellu-
losic materials, as well as some minor quantities of primary 
sugars, starch, proteins, and lipids. The chemical composi -
tion of such lignocelluloses is interconnected through non-
covalent forces or covalent linkages, with compositions 
varying across plant species [9]. Ultimate analysis revealed 
the chemical composition of the biomass, including hydro -
gen, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and trace amounts of sul -
fur and chlorine. Burning biomass is a common method 
of energy liberation, which can also be transformed into 
other usable energy forms, including ethanol and biodiesel. 
Methane gas, a key natural gas component, can be derived 
from sources such as rotten garbage and agricultural and 
human waste, often referred to as landfill gas or biogas. In 
comparison to different advanced materials for electrodes, 
such as carbon nanotubes (CNT) and graphene, carbons 
derived from biomass offer various key applications. These 
include cost-effectiveness due to the abundance of biomass-
derived carbon precursors. Additionally, the in situ porous 
nano structure evolution preserves the bio-macromolecular 
frame during the conversion to carbon in the protection of 
inert gas, resulting in inter-connected conductive structures. 
Furthermore, the variability in processing and outcome is 
noteworthy, as different types of bio-precursors can be trans-
formed into carbons derived from biomass through similar 
processing methods, including carbonization, activation, 
and purification. Moreover, the introduction of various 
chemicals, including metallic compounds, during the con -
version process further enhances the electrochemical and 
catalytic properties of the biomass-derived carbons. Lastly, 
the fabrication does not require a high-temperature environ-
ment or harmful chemicals, unlike the process of synthesis 
of graphene, CNT, etc [ 9, 12, 13]. Understanding the sur -
face phenomena is crucial for optimizing energy storage

 In addition to other carbon allotropes, we present car -
byne, which is a theoretical form characterized by a linear 
chain of carbon atoms. Each carbon atom in this structure is 
bonded to two neighboring carbon atoms through a chain of 
alternating single and triple bonds, as depicted in Fig. 7(a). 
Carbyne’s theoretical promise in SCs lies in its exceptional 
tensile strength and potential for 1D electron delocaliza -
tion. Carbon atoms can be arranged in specific configura -
tions based on the type of bond between them. When carbon 
atoms are arranged alternately with double and triple bonds, 
as depicted in Fig. 7(b), they are referred to as α-carbyne 
or cumulene. Conversely, when the arrangement consists of 
single and triple bonds, as depicted in Fig. 7(c), it is referred 
to as ꞵ-carbyne or polyyne. Carbyne is often regarded as 
a unique carbon nanostructure, distinguished by its supe -
rior strength and stiffness compared to those of graphene 
and CNTs. Furthermore, it is recognized for its exceptional 
electrical, thermal, and mechanical properties, making it a 
subject of significant interest in material science research. 
However, the synthesis of this material in its pure form 
remains a significant challenge because of its high reactiv -
ity and instability. Researchers are diligently working to 
develop methods for stabilizing and isolating carbynes, with 
the aim of exploring their potential applications. However, 
Stabilization strategies for carbyne include encapsulation 
and in-situ synthesis on substrates [40, 43, 45, 46].

Graphite has emerged as a crucial source material in various 
applications such as microsensors, energy devices, super 
adsorbents, and semiconductors. Several methods have 
experimental findings show that a high specific area of over 
3,000 m2 g− 1 yields small EDLC values of < 10 µF cm − 2. 
This suggests that none of the pores effectively contribute to 
the accumulation of charge [44, 45]. However, pore accessi-
bility, rather than sheer surface area, governs effective EDL 
capacitance, whereas, misalignment between ion size and 
pore dimensions can severely reduce capacitance and ion 
mobility.
1-D frameworks
Compared to 0-dimensional carbon nanoparticles, 1-dimen-
sional carbon materials show prominence as electrode 
materials in SC because they have extended 1-dimensional 
nanostructure, which in turn supports the emergence of a 
continuous network for charge transport. Carbon nano-
tubes (CNTs), which include single- and multi-walled mate-
rials, are among the most common 1-dimensional carbon 
materials and demonstrate significantly higher conductivity 
than AC. However, despite surface treatments, their specific 
capacitance remains limited to just over 100 Fg − 1  when 
obsessed with the energy storage potential [ 46]. Moreover, 
CNTs offer superior conductivity but limited capacitance due 
to low surface functionalization and entanglement effects. 
Alignment of CNTs remains a key factor in achieving high-
rate performance in SC applications. 1D Carbon nano-fibers 
(CNFs) derived from biomass such as flax and cotton offer 
a scalable path toward green nanostructured electrodes. An 
electrode utilizing ZnCl 2-activated CNFs showed a spe -
cific capacity of 214 Fg − 1, retaining 97.3% of its capaci -
tance over 60,000 cycles [47]. A variety of fibrous biomass 
materials, such as flax, cotton, wood, and ramie, have been 
employed as precursors for production of one-dimensional 
(1-D) carbon. Cellulose, in particular, has emerged as the 
most extensively researched and utilized material, such as

3-D frameworks
The increase in dimensions led to a higher percentage of 
active area over the surface available to interact with the 
electrolyte, thereby enhancing the electrochemical kinet -
ics by reducing the diffusion pathways. 3D carbon aerogels 
provide interconnected pathways that reduce resistance and 
support high rate performance. Carbon 3-D nanostructures 
without any substrates show promise for SCs with bet -
ter efficiency, as the use of substrates adds weight to the 
devices and hampers improvements in gravimetric specific 
energy and power. Biomass-derived 3D carbons maintain 
macroscopic structural integrity after carbonization. Pore-
size distribution in 3D networks can be tuned via templating 
or activation conditions. Simple carbonization of cotton fol-
lowed by KOH activation produced a flexible fiber aerogel 
been employed to process graphite into reduced-graphene 
oxide (rGO). Some of these techniques are eco-friendly and 
do not involve the use of polymers or surfactants. However, 
the use of ammonia in certain methods raises concerns, par-
ticularly in large-scale applications. Microwave treatment 
has been utilized for the exfoliation of graphite oxide into 
rGO. A non-toxic technique involving microwave reduction 
of GO assisted by an ionic liquid has demonstrated a spe -
cific capacity of 135 Fg − 1 and has been noted for its rapid 
and facile nature [50, 51].
The exfoliation of graphite using Gum Arabic and ultra -
sonication results in partial graphene production. Gra -
phene’s electrical properties stem from its 2D sp 2 carbon 
lattice and Dirac electron dispersion. However, achieving 
100% pure graphene required 100 h of ultrasonication 
and acid treatment. Similarly, attempts have been made to 
develop green techniques for processing rGO, which typi -
cally involve complex processes for removing the reducing 
agents. Efficiently, with the use of sodium carbonate, rGO 
can be obtained from graphene oxide, albeit requiring a 
4-hour reduction period [52]. The use of graphene as a mate-
rial for electrodes in SCs is primarily owing to its distinctive 
properties. Graphene possesses a honeycomb lattice struc -
ture consisting of two carbon atom sublattices held in pairs 
with σ bonds. While graphene’s single layer of atoms with 
a good specific area is a suitable material for electrodes, the 
complete removal of functional groups and heteroatoms can 
impact its capacitance as heteroatom doping of graphene 
can tailor its bandgap and modulate its interaction with 
electrolyte species. Graphene’s theoretical specific area is 
known to be 2630 m 2 g − 1 , and experimentally, rGO has 
achieved 2687 m2 g− 1. Layered graphene showed a specific 
surface area of 1400 m2 g− 1 and was porous when a micro-
wave technique was implemented [ 53, 54]. Graphene and 
rGO exhibit slight structural differences, primarily attrib -
uted to the existence of lattice defects in greater numbers

Cyclic voltammetry
Over a potential window ranging from V 1 to V 2, a 
time-dependent current and potential, represented by 
i = C (dV /dt), is observed as a waveform, as depicted in 
Fig. 9(a). This response, known as cyclic voltammetry (CV), 
effectively characterizes the capacitor type. A near-ideal CV 
profile indicates capacitive charge storage dominated by 
EDLC behavior, reflecting their non-faradaic nature. How -
ever, high ESR results in distorted CV profiles and limits 
power density in practical devices owing to the properties 
of the materials used (Fig. 9(b)) [44].
